text: You get two integers, n and k. Return all possible combinations of k numbers chosen from the range one to n. Any order is fine.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — one, two and two, one are the same combination, so I return it only once. And each number is used at most once inside one combination. Is that right?
Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is between one and twenty, and k is between one and n.

Okay. Since k is at most n, there is always at least one answer. I never return an empty list. Let me run through the example. n equals four, k equals two gives one-two, one-three, one-four, two-three, two-four, and three-four. That's six pairs. And n equals one, k equals one gives just one.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to go through every bitmask from zero to two to the n minus one, and keep the ones with exactly k bits set. It's simple, and I'll use it later as a checker. But it looks at every subset, even the wrong sizes. This problem reminds me of the backtracking template for building subsets with a start index: each level only picks numbers bigger than the last one. Here I only record a path when it has exactly k numbers.

Here's the plan. One: keep a path, and a start s, the smallest number I may still pick. Two: if the path has k numbers, record it and return. Three: otherwise loop i from s to n, push i, recurse with i plus one, and pop. Here, I'm using s to keep track of the next number I'm allowed to pick. Every path is strictly increasing, so one, two can appear, but two, one never does, and no number repeats. One thing worth flagging — the numbers are one through n, not zero through n minus one. So the first call starts at one, and the loop runs while i is at most n. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I'll think out loud as I go. The main function starts the search at one. The search records the path once it has k numbers; otherwise it loops i from s up to n, inclusive, pushes i, recurses with i plus one, and pops. Path is passed by reference. There's one shared path, and the push and pop pair puts it back the way it was. I only copy it when I record an answer. The return after recording matters for speed. Once the path has k numbers, there's nothing more to add on that branch.
This works. Can you prune it? Some branches can never reach k numbers.

Let me walk through that. Right. At each call I still need k minus path size more numbers. If I start at i, the numbers left are i through n — that's n minus i plus one numbers. If that's less than what I need, the branch is dead. Keeping i only when enough numbers are left gives a new loop bound: i at most n minus need plus one. So I only change the loop. One thing worth flagging — the plus one is a correctness point, not style. i through n is an inclusive range, so its size is n minus i plus one. Drop the plus one and the last valid start gets cut. For n equals one, k equals one, the bound becomes i at most zero, the loop never runs, and I return an empty list.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. n equals four, k equals three, expected one-two-three, one-two-four, one-three-four, and two-three-four. My first version makes fifteen calls, and five of them can never reach size three. The pruned version cuts all five and makes ten calls. The row that matters is call one: it needs three numbers, so the bound is four minus three plus one, which is two. Starting at three leaves only three and four, which is too few. Both versions return the same answer. Corner cases: n one, k one gives just one. Recursing with i makes n two, k two return one-one, one-two, and two-two. Recursing with s plus one returns one-two and two-two. The bound without the plus one returns nothing for n one, k one. Against the bitmask version, on all 55 cases with n up to ten: zero wrong.

Let me think about complexity here. With pruning, time is k times C of n, k. There are C of n, k answers, copying each one costs k, and every call is on a path that leads to an answer, so the work is bound by the output. Space is O of k extra for the recursion stack and the path, not counting the output. The worst case for my first version is k close to n. Take n twenty, k eighteen: only 190 answers, but no pruning makes 1,048,555 calls, almost two to the twentieth, in 6.35 milliseconds. Pruned, it's 1,330 calls in 0.017 milliseconds. Oh, one more thing — the biggest output is n twenty, k ten: 184,756 answers. There, pruning still helps, but less: 616,666 versus 352,716 calls. And for k equals two, it's 211 versus 210. Pruning only pays off when k is large.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You derived the pruning bound from counting the n minus i plus one numbers left, not from guessing. You knew the plus one is a correctness point, and had n one, k one returning nothing ready as proof. And you told apart i plus one, i, and s plus one with a small case each. Good work.
